fixes.answer: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a [[vital outlet]] for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].
fixes.why: 'balanced' and 'fulfilling' are plain; marked 'vital outlet' and 'nourishing'

fixes.answer: There are noticeable differences. Older generations often favour traditional [[pastimes]] like gardening, reading physical books, or socialising in person. Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. So the core need for leisure is universal, but the [[medium]] has shifted towards the digital.

Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that [[enrich]] other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.
fixes.why: 4 marks with plain 'match' and 'rewarding'; kept 'enrich' and marked 'therapeutic' and 'nourish the soul'

fixes.answer: Free time is essential for a good quality of life. It provides the space to rest, [[recharge]] and pursue the activities and relationships that bring us joy and meaning. Without adequate leisure, people risk burnout, stress and a [[diminished]] sense of wellbeing. Free time allows us to be more than just workers. So I would argue that leisure is not a luxury but a fundamental necessity for a healthy, [[rounded]] existence.

This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that [[constant connectivity]] and economic pressure could actually [[erode]] our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.
fixes.why: 'choices' and 'priorities' are plain; marked 'optimistically' and 'constant connectivity'

fixes.answer: It often comes down to priorities rather than an absolute lack of time. People can start by consciously [[carving out]] even small [[pockets of time]], perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. Scheduling hobby time like any other commitment helps make it happen. Choosing hobbies that fit their lifestyle is also wise. Essentially, treating leisure as essential rather than optional helps people [[reclaim]] time they did not realise they had.
fixes.why: 'had' and 'essential' are plain; marked 'carving out' and 'pockets of time'

fixes.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].
fixes.why: 'useful' and 'pleasure' are plain; marked 'worthwhile' and 'exactly the point'
